                                                        Abstract
     The vast majority of optimization and online learning algorithms today require some prior infor-
     mation about the data (often in the form of bounds on gradients or on the optimal parameter value).
     When this information is not available, these algorithms require laborious manual tuning of vari-
     ous hyperparameters, motivating the search for algorithms that can adapt to the data with no prior
     information. We describe a frontier of new lower bounds on the performance of such algorithms,
     reflecting a tradeoff between a term that depends on the optimal parameter value and a term that
     depends on the gradients’ rate of growth. Further, we construct a family of algorithms whose
     performance matches any desired point on this frontier, which no previous algorithm reaches.

2. Notation and Setup
Before proceeding further, we provide a few definitions that will be useful throughout this paper.
A set W is a convex set if W is a subset of some real vector space and tx + (1 − t)y ∈ W for all
x, y ∈ W and t ∈ [0, 1]. Throughout this paper we will assume that W is closed. A function f is a
convex function if f (tx + (1 − t)y) ≥ tf (x) + (1 − t)f (y) for all x, y and t ∈ [0, 1]. If f : V → R
for some vector space V , then a vector g ∈ V ∗ is a subgradient of f at x, denoted g ∈ ∂f (x), if
f (y) ≥ f (x) + g · (y − x) for all y. Here we use the dot product to indicate application of linear
functionals in the dual space since this should cause no confusion. A norm k · k is a function such
that kxk = 0 if and only if x = 0, kcxk = |c|kxk for any scalar c, and kx + yk ≤ kxk + kyk for all
x and y. The dual norm is a norm k · k? defined by kxk? = supkyk=1 x · y. As a special case, when

kxk = x · x (the L2 norm), then k · k? = k · k.
     Online convex optimization problems can be reduced to online linear optimization problems in
which the loss functions are constrained to be linear functions. The reduction follows by replacing
the loss function `t (w) with the linear function gt · w, where gt is a subgradient of `t at wt . Then,
by definition, gt · wt − gt · u ≥ `t (wt ) − `t (u). Therefore the regret of our algorithm with respect to
the linear loss functions gt · w is an upper-bound on the regret with respect to the real loss functions
`t . Because of this reduction, many online convex optimization algorithms (including ours) are first
order algorithms, meaning they access the loss functions only through their subgradients. For the
rest of this paper we will therefore assume that the losses are linear, `t (w) = gt · w.
     We will focus all of our lower bounds in Section 3 and algorithms in Section 5 on the case in

This case is very common in practical optimization optimization problems encountered in machine

Since our analysis does not make assumptions about the loss functions or comparison point u, the
parameters k and γ can be freely chosen by the user. Unlike other algorithms that require kuk or
Lmax , there are no unknown constraints on these parameters.
